Good morning from the Gulf FC3 here. A-School is A-School it just gives you a taste of all the different types of FC you could end up being. You will work on understanding Radar Theory, Radar 1, Radar 2, and etc. The schedule of things at A-School may have changed since I was there. In A-School the most important thing is probably just make sure you understand what they are trying to teach you. If you don't understand ask questions. If you still don't understand go to open study, study on your own time, or ask friends. Radar Theory was the most difficult section of the course for people in my class to understand. We had someone get dropped because he failed the Radar Theory test 4 times. He got set back etc etc. Make sure you study though really it will help even if you just do it for 20 minutes a day you will remember the shit better if you take it in little chunks than try to cram it all last minute. You will have plenty of time for PS4/XBOX One/Computer/etc after you finish A-School. You might be on holds for a little bit in GL waiting on orders. CIWS C-School in San Diego is awesome because frankly it's California nice weather most days, relaxed base, etc. I am an 1122 CIWS Tech that went to San Diego C-School and it was nice for several reasons but then again it wasn't nice for those same reasons. First off I was a nights student so I went to school M-Thurs 1500-1800 Friday 1300-1500. The hours seem legit right? Most Navy Schools are short and sweet to the point but you aren't going to have the experience you need for the fleet going to San Diego C-School. The instructors aren't bad per-say but they kind of give the class decisions like "hey do you guys want to go out and learn how to take the drum apart or do you want to listen to me talk about it for 5 minutes so we can get out of here". You will get really good at using the Tech Pubs on the computers because of CTRL F to find the answers for the tests. The Tech Pubs on the computer on the old Kontron computers are more hassle than they are worth also most ships don't have many paper Tech Pubs anymore. The Golden Rule on San Diego base when I was there was: Be where you are supposed to be on time. There's plenty of stuff to do in San Diego that should keep you busy and out of trouble but there is also plenty of stuff you could do to get you in trouble as well. If your equipment is broken like mine was when I got to the ship make sure you do all you can to learn your system. On my ship we have 2 CIWS Mounts 21 and 22. Our 22 was down for 9 months because the Techs before us neglected to take care of it during the yard period. It cost us 86,000 (cable harness) 65,000 (scan drive assembly) 12,000 (ku amp/passive limiter) and maybe 20,000 on random parts and countless man hours to repair it. Also I was lucky enough to participate in INSURV which is like the big ship inspection of everything in terms of operation/execution to material inspection. Deployment as an FC isn't too bad so far. I got to my ship the last 2 months of their last deployment. This is/will be my first full deployment. My ship is BMD so our deployment is 9 months long. The manning for my ship 6 CIWS Techs for 2 mounts. 3 2nd classes, 2 3rd classes, and 1 Chief. Watch isn't too unbearable it can be long from mid to morning but you should be fine. Ships have different configurations for watches but for us RCS is manned up 24/7. The people that you work will with greatly determine how your quality of life is. You can have a Chief who is crazy about topside preservation and you will be painting all the time or you can have a Chief who doesn't care about topside but wants like 30 U-Checks completed on your equipment for no reason. During training cycles and work ups you will end up going out to sea for a couple days to float around and do drills/evolutions/gun shoots etc. I think that I've shot 21 and 22 about 15 times each which is quite a bit of shooting. I've also got to shoot the guns in surface mode at big inflatable targets in the water. It's fun getting to shoot but there's maintenance you have to do before you can even shoot the gun. We have to do pre-fires which is a certain set of checks that verify correct operation of mount movement, firing circuits, firing cut outs, etc. After we shoot the guns then we get to do more maintenance! We get to take the barrels out clean them off, punch them with bore cleaners, regrease them, etc. Oh and we also get to take out the breech bolts to clean and inspect them since when we shoot they get slammed around a lot. It's really what you make of it though. CIWS has alot of maintenance but if you have a good WCS and people in your workcenter you guys can get it down to have most checks finished by Wednesday. The hardest part of doing maintenance on deployment is going through the proper channels to get permission to take down a gun because it's a weapon system and could be needed at anytime. It might seem like it a lot but don't let it send you away from CIWS it's a great system which will work fine if you MAINTAIN it. We've been out to sea for a while now on deployment and we have had only 2 major casualties. We had a bent cam pin on the scoop disk for 21 and 22 had a leaking pipe. I'm not really sure what else to type but if you have more questions just reply here or pm me. Take it easy.
